notes: Bankruptcy costs appeal; consent annulment and service of statutory demand.

enrichment.short_title: Bankruptcy costs after consent annulment of VAT petition
key_facts: Mr Housiaux, a VAT-registered electrical retailer, failed to pay VAT assessments and a statutory demand was served at his shop address through the letterbox.
His wife collected the demand and petition but did not tell him; a bankruptcy order was made in his absence in December 1999.
The bankruptcy was annulled by consent in February 2000 on the basis the order ought not to have been made, but costs of the petition and annulment were reserved.
District Judge Fink ordered Mr and Mrs Housiaux to pay those costs; Peter Smith J dismissed their appeal and Chadwick LJ dismissed the second appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal against costs orders following annulment of a bankruptcy order made on a Customs & Excise VAT petition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs assessed at £5,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where a bankruptcy order is annulled because the debtor did not know of the statutory demand or petition, the court retains a broad discretion on costs; failure of internal communication between spouses about documents left at the registered VAT office does not entitle the debtor to recover costs from the petitioning creditor, and procedural defects in service do not automatically shift costs to the creditor.
legal_issues: Discretion to order costs against a debtor who successfully annulled a bankruptcy order under section 282(1)(a)
Whether service of statutory demand through letterbox at registered VAT address was effective
Effect of consent annulment order without admission of liability
Whether district judge should have heard oral evidence on disputed facts

notes: Public services procurement regulations; reg 32(4)(a) letter before action; misfeasance.

enrichment.short_title: Local authority pre-tender exclusion and procurement regulations
key_facts: Gary Luck, a long-standing arboricultural contractor to Tower Hamlets, applied to tender for a consolidated tree maintenance contract but was excluded at pre-tender stage.
A critical corporate reference compiled by Mr Ford, based on information from council officers, was central to the exclusion decision.
Luck claimed breach of the Public Services Contracts Regulations 1993 and misfeasance in public office, alleging bad faith by officers who supplied information for the reference.
The court held Luck failed reg 32(4)(a) because pre-writ correspondence did not identify the specific regulation or breach, and the contract was not property management services within Part A.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from trial judgment dismissing claim for damages after contractor excluded from invitation to tender for public services contract.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; leave to appeal to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 32(4)(a) requires a services provider to inform the contracting authority of the specific breach and intention to bring proceedings under that regulation before suing; a generic letter before action is insufficient, and that requirement is valid under EU equivalence and effectiveness principles and Article 6 ECHR; inferred bad faith is defeated where the authority's decision was within the range of reasonable responses.
legal_issues: Validity and construction of regulation 32(4)(a) notice requirement
Whether tree maintenance contract was property management services under Schedule 1
Publication of minimum standards under regulations 11(8) and 12(4)
Bad faith and misfeasance where decision appears reasonable on its face

notes: All-risks policy; waste clause warranty breach barred material damage and BI claims.

enrichment.short_title: Restaurant fire claim barred by waste clause warranty
key_facts: Soho Pizzeria held a combined all-risks policy with AXA covering material damage and business interruption for premises at Beak Street.
A fire on 11 April 2001 after closing caused agreed losses of about £289,400, but AXA relied on endorsement GO3 (the waste clause) as a warranty.
Forensic evidence showed the fire started in a preparation-area waste bin containing trade waste and a discarded cigarette end.
Staff had left by 0030 without fully clearing the bin despite a practice of removing bagged waste to the street before vacating.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for indemnity under material damage and business interruption sections of combined all-risks policy.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; non-compliance with waste clause warranty increased fire risk and barred the claim under General Condition 13.
enrichment.ratio: Under a material damage waste clause warranty requiring daily sweeping, bagging and removal of trade waste to a secure disposal area before premises are vacated, leaving combustible trade waste overnight in an on-premises bin increases the risk of fire; under General Condition 13 non-compliance that increases risk bars claims even where the insured was unaware of the warranty.
legal_issues: Construction of waste clause sub-clauses on greasy cloths and trade waste
Whether on-premises bin could be a secure waste disposal area
Whether breach increased risk of fire sufficiently to bar claim
Meaning of trade waste in restaurant context

notes: Forward freight swap repudiatory breach; available market damages at termination date.

enrichment.short_title: Forward freight swap damages after counterparty insolvency
key_facts: Norden chartered in the Panamax bulk carrier Talisman and hedged with a 12-month forward freight swap (FFA) with Andre at a fixed rate of $10,675 per day.
Andre lost credit lines and entered Swiss insolvency proceedings in March 2001; Norden terminated the FFA for breach of continuing solvency warranties.
Norden claimed damages of about $757,386 based on full contract performance; Andre argued replacement FFA available at about $10,000, limiting loss to $185,625.
Expert evidence showed an available market; damages assessed at date of termination as $192,500 ($700 per day over 275 days).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial to assess damages after Andre conceded Norden validly terminated forward freight swap on 19 March 2001.
enrichment.outcome: Damages assessed at $192,500 excluding interest, not the higher figure claimed by Norden.
enrichment.ratio: Where a contract is wrongfully repudiated and there is an available substitute market, damages are prima facie the difference between the contract rate and the market replacement rate at the date of termination; it is not enough that the innocent party reasonably chose not to replace the contract or faced uncertainty about the validity of termination or the guilty party's ability to pay.
legal_issues: Whether an available market existed for replacement FFAs in March 2001
Application of Elena D'Amico market differential measure to FFAs
Whether Norden reasonably declined to enter replacement hedge
Date for assessing market differential (termination vs end of March)

notes: Partial allowance of strike-out appeal; victimisation claim against BBC solicitor remitted.

enrichment.short_title: Race discrimination strike-out of BBC harassment claim
key_facts: Dr Jiad, a BBC Arabic Service producer, alleged harassment by BBC solicitor Janet Youngson on 7 February 2000 and failure by senior managers to investigate.
He claimed direct racial discrimination and victimisation under the Race Relations Act 1976 against four individual respondents, not the BBC.
Employment tribunal struck out the claim as scandalous, frivolous or vexatious and ordered costs; EAT upheld the strike-out.
Court of Appeal held claims against Byford, Grainger and Dyke bound to fail but victimisation claim against Youngson should proceed to trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal upholding strike-out of employment tribunal race discrimination and victimisation claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; claim against Janet Youngson remitted; strike-out upheld against other three respondents; costs orders varied.
enrichment.ratio: Discrimination claims should rarely be struck out except where bound to fail; a victimisation claim alleging bullying by a solicitor with litigation history against the claimant is not necessarily bound to fail for want of comparator, and alleged psychological detriment supported by GP treatment may be sufficient to cross the threshold for trial despite being weak.
legal_issues: Test for strike-out under employment tribunal rule 13(2)(d)
Meaning of detriment under section 4(2)(c)
Need for actual or hypothetical comparator in victimisation
Whether failure to investigate can amount to discrimination

notes: Legal aid funding review quashed for failure to address Clement Jones negligence causation.

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid certificate discharge review quashed for inadequate reasons
key_facts: Patricia Dixon held legal aid to sue former solicitors Clement Jones for negligence in handling a claim against accountants Dyers over a failed convenience store venture.
Legal aid was discharged in February 1997 after counsel advised prospects were poor, partly because an expert accountant report did not address Londis profit projections.
Funding review committee dismissed Dixon's appeal against 2002 certificate discharge, treating earlier 1997 discharge as a formidable obstacle.
Hooper J quashed the decision because the committee failed to address whether Clement Jones' negligence caused the 1997 discharge and whether competent evidence would have continued funding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Legal Services Commission funding review committee decision dismissing appeal against discharge of legal aid certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed and remitted to another funding review committee; inter partes costs order made with 20% reduction after one month from witness statement.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant's case against former solicitors is that negligent failure to obtain proper expert evidence caused an earlier legal aid discharge, a funding review committee must analyse that causation issue; failure to address the central argument in the decision letter or chairman's witness statement renders the decision unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether committee misunderstood counsel's lost-chance assessment as applying to Clement Jones claim
Adequacy of reasons for rejecting 50-50 prospects assessment
Effect of 1997 legal aid discharge on later negligence claim against solicitors
Procedural fairness and adequacy of documentation before committee

notes: Youth court committal to Crown Court quashed; section 91 route inappropriate for 13-year-old.

enrichment.short_title: Youth court wrongly committed 13-year-old robber to Crown Court
key_facts: A 13-year-old boy was charged with robbery arising from a park incident two days after his thirteenth birthday, involving demand for money and punches causing minor injuries.
Leeds Youth Court committed him to the Crown Court under section 24(1)(a) on the basis section 91(3) detention might be possible if convicted.
He was not a persistent offender so a detention and training order under section 100(2) could not be made.
Following R v Sheffield Youth Court and related authorities, committal was quashed and the case remitted for summary trial in the youth court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review (with extension of time) of youth court decision committing child to Crown Court for trial.
enrichment.outcome: Committal order quashed; case remitted to Youth Court with direction to proceed with summary trial; claimant's costs from central funds.
enrichment.ratio: Section 24(1)(a) committal for grave crimes under section 91(3) should not be used as a route to custodial sentence where a detention and training order cannot be made because the offender is under 15 and not a persistent offender; youth courts are generally the appropriate forum for young defendants.
legal_issues: Construction of section 24(1)(a) Magistrates' Courts Act 1980
Relationship between section 91 and section 100 Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000
When Crown Court committal appropriate for under-15 defendant
Application of Sheffield Youth Court line of authority

notes: DLA supersession requires finding of relevant change of circumstances; appeal allowed.

enrichment.short_title: Disability benefit supersession without change of circumstances

statutes_considered.title: Social Security and Child Support (Decisions and Appeals) Regulations 1999
Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mr Wood had a life award of mobility allowance converted to higher-rate DLA mobility component for cerebral palsy from 1992.
In December 2000 his advisers applied to supersede the award for increased care needs only; medical evidence showed his condition was permanent.
Secretary of State superseded the decision in March 2001 and removed both care and mobility components, finding he could walk 400-1000 metres.
Appeal tribunal did not consider whether mobility had changed since the life award; Commissioner remitted case but court held supersession unlawful without change-of-circumstances finding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal from Social Security Commissioner's decision on lawfulness of supersession removing DLA mobility component.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to appeal tribunal to determine whether relevant change of circumstances existed.
enrichment.ratio: An existing benefit award may only be superseded under section 10 of the Social Security Act 1998 if a regulation 6 criterion is established in fact, including a relevant change of circumstances; the Secretary of State cannot revisit entitlement on merits alone without such a finding, and a tribunal must determine change of circumstances before assessing virtually unable to walk.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 6(2) sets threshold or outcome criteria
Need for factual finding of relevant change of circumstances before supersession
Construction of section 12(9) right of appeal from supersession decisions
Meaning of supersede in section 10 scheme

notes: Student IDI Chapter 4 authorises part-time work for leave-to-enter-as-student holders.

enrichment.short_title: Student part-time work authorised by immigration IDI
key_facts: Mr Zhou, a Chinese national with leave to enter as a student, worked 12 hours weekly at Waitrose while studying at Brooklands College.
Brooklands reported poor attendance and his part-time work to the Immigration Service; removal directions were issued for breach of Code 2 employment conditions.
Secretary of State contended poor attendance meant Zhou was no longer a student so IDI Annex A Chapter 4 part-time work authorisation did not apply.
Court held student in Chapter 4 means anyone with leave to enter as a student for the granted period, so part-time work was authorised and removal unlawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of permission for judicial review; court granted permission and determined judicial review on merits.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; decision to remove quashed; Secretary of State to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: In Immigration Directorates' Instructions Annex A Chapter 4, student means a person who has been given leave to enter or remain as a student for the currency of that leave, not someone who continues to meet paragraph 57 HC 395 attendance requirements; such a person on Code 2 conditions may work part-time without separate authorisation.
legal_issues: Construction of student in IDI Chapter 4
Whether poor attendance terminates student status for employment purposes
Lawfulness of section 10 removal for unauthorised employment
Relationship between HC 395 paragraph 57 and IDI employment guidance

notes: Sugar FFA put options unenforceable under Financial Services Act 1986; section 69 appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Sugar put options unenforceable as unauthorised investment business
key_facts: CR Sugar paid substantial premiums to CSW for put options to sell raw sugar, used by CR's affiliate to hedge New York futures positions.
Parties intended options would be rolled over without physical delivery; when market fell CR exercised options creating C&F sale contracts CSW refused to perform.
Sugar Association arbitrators held contracts were investment business under the Financial Services Act 1986 and unenforceable because CR was unauthorised.
Parties had no intention to deliver sugar at time options were granted; tribunal found contracts made for investment not commercial purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 69 appeal with permission against arbitration award holding sugar sale contracts unenforceable under Financial Services Act 1986.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 68 application allowed by consent on quantum; section 5 relief application struck out.
enrichment.ratio: Commodity options and resulting sale contracts are investments under the Financial Services Act 1986; where parties at grant of put options did not intend physical delivery and planned roll-overs for hedging profit, Note (4) to Schedule 1 paragraph 8 indicates investment rather than commercial purpose, rendering contracts unenforceable against an unauthorised UK counterparty under section 5(1)(a).
legal_issues: Whether put options and C&F contracts were investments under Schedule 1
Commercial vs investment purpose under Note (4) to paragraph 8
Relevant date for assessing intention to deliver
Whether arbitrators could grant section 5(3) relief and whether court could hear late section 5 application
